--- title: "Mosquito density and EIR" --- Larviciding, a wetter decade and a new irrigation scheme all act on the size of the mosquito population rather than through the nets, and `estimate_eir_with_mosquito_delta` is the estimator for that class of change. It takes a measured prevalence, a setting and a fractional change in mosquito density, and returns the EIR the setting settles at once the new density holds. That is an equilibrium value, not a trajectory. ## The signature ```python estimate_eir_with_mosquito_delta(inputs: pd.DataFrame, *, models: dict) -> pd.DataFrame ``` `inputs` carries one row per scenario and eight columns, `prevalence`, `mosquito_delta`, and the six setting covariates `dn0_use`, `Q0`, `phi_bednets`, `seasonal`, `itn_use` and `irs_use`. `models` is keyword-only. It must hold all three models, under the keys `"prevalence"`, `"hbr"` and `"eir_to_hbr"`. `mosquito_delta` is a fraction rather than a multiplier, so `0.25` is a 25% increase, `-0.5` a halving and `0.0` no change. It must be greater than `-1`. ::: {.callout-warning} ## A note on the older signature estiMINT 1.4 accepted loose keyword arguments such as `prevalence=...` and `dn0_use=...`, one call per scenario, and loaded the models itself. That form has been removed. The current call takes a **DataFrame** and an explicit **`models` dict**, and it is vectorised, so pass every scenario as a row of one frame rather than looping. ::: ## The ratio method The method runs in five steps, and the reason for each is given in [EIR and HBR](eir-and-hbr.qmd). 1. The prevalence and the setting give a **baseline EIR**, via the prevalence model. 2. That EIR and the setting give a **baseline HBR**, via `eir_to_hbr`. 3. The **new HBR** is the baseline scaled by the density change, `hbr_new = hbr_baseline * (1 + mosquito_delta)`. Density enters here, and only here. 4. The `hbr` model predicts an EIR at **both** HBR values, the baseline and the new one. 5. The **new EIR** is the *baseline* EIR times the **ratio** of those two predictions. The EIR the `hbr` model predicts at `hbr_new` is not itself the answer, because every prediction from that model inherits the round-trip bias measured in [EIR and HBR](eir-and-hbr.qmd), where an EIR of 13.40 put through both models comes back as 14.23. Taking a ratio cancels it. What survives is the *relative* response of EIR to a change in biting, applied to a baseline EIR the prevalence model produced without touching the HBR models. ## A density sweep The setting from [Estimating EIR from prevalence](estimating-eir.qmd), at a prevalence of 0.30, runs over five density changes, a halving of the mosquitoes, a cut of a quarter, no change at all, and two increases. ::: {#b387f7cb .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from estimint import load_xgb_model, estimate_eir_with_mosquito_delta models = { "prevalence": load_xgb_model("prevalence"), "hbr": load_xgb_model("hbr"), "eir_to_hbr": load_xgb_model("eir_to_hbr"), } setting = dict( dn0_use=0.33, Q0=0.87, phi_bednets=0.82, seasonal=0.0, itn_use=0.6, irs_use=0.0, ) inputs = pd.DataFrame([ {"prevalence": 0.30, "mosquito_delta": d, **setting} for d in [-0.5, -0.25, 0.0, 0.25, 0.6] ]) result = estimate_eir_with_mosquito_delta(inputs, models=models) result.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
eir_baseline eir_new eir_multiplier hbr_baseline hbr_new
0 13.397 5.807 0.433 238818.554 119409.277
1 13.397 9.523 0.711 238818.554 179113.915
2 13.397 13.397 1.000 238818.554 238818.554
3 13.397 16.882 1.260 238818.554 298523.192
4 13.397 20.869 1.558 238818.554 382109.686
``` ::: ::: The frame comes back on the same index as `inputs`, so the delta that produced each row joins straight back on. ::: {#e91b665e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} summary = inputs[["mosquito_delta"]].join(result[["eir_baseline", "eir_new", "eir_multiplier"]]) summary.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
mosquito_delta eir_baseline eir_new eir_multiplier
0 -0.50 13.397 5.807 0.433
1 -0.25 13.397 9.523 0.711
2 0.00 13.397 13.397 1.000
3 0.25 13.397 16.882 1.260
4 0.60 13.397 20.869 1.558
``` ::: ::: `eir_baseline` is identical down the column, as it must be, because the prevalence and the setting did not change and only the mosquitoes did. Halving the vector population takes the EIR from about 13.4 to about 5.8. A 60% rise takes it to about 20.9. ## The EIR multiplier Halving the mosquitoes cuts the EIR by rather more than half, a multiplier of 0.43 rather than 0.50, while a 60% increase raises it by rather less than 60%, a multiplier of 1.56 rather than 1.60. Plotting the multiplier against a proportional reference shows where the two part company. ::: {#9bc0842b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np grid = pd.DataFrame([ {"prevalence": 0.30, "mosquito_delta": d, **setting} for d in np.linspace(-0.75, 1.0, 36) ]) curve = estimate_eir_with_mosquito_delta(grid, models=models) fig, ax = plt.subplots() ax.plot(grid["mosquito_delta"], curve["eir_multiplier"], label="EIR multiplier") ax.plot(grid["mosquito_delta"], 1 + grid["mosquito_delta"], ls="--", label="proportional response") ax.axhline(1.0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7) ax.set_xlabel("Mosquito density change (mosquito_delta)") ax.set_ylabel("EIR multiplier") ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![EIR multiplier against fractional change in mosquito density, compared with a proportional response.](mosquito-density_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){fig-alt='The EIR multiplier rises from about 0.2 at a 75% reduction in mosquitoes to about 1.9 at a doubling. It tracks the dashed proportional reference line closely near zero but falls clearly below it at both extremes.'} ::: ::: The blue multiplier curve sits on the dashed green proportional line for modest changes either side of zero, and within about 10% in each direction a proportional response is accurate to a percent or so. At both extremes the blue curve drops below the green one. This is because deep cuts take the EIR down faster than they take the mosquitoes, so removing three quarters of them leaves about a fifth of the baseline EIR rather than a quarter. Large increases run the other way. A doubling of the vector population falls short of doubling transmission. The gap is a few percent rather than a factor. It is why the response is read off the model instead of assumed linear, and why `eir_multiplier` comes back beside the EIR. ::: {.callout-warning} ## A note on the input mode `mosquito_delta` is honoured when the driving input is a **prevalence**. In the scenario API of [Running scenarios](../06-scenarios/run-scenarios.qmd), where the input mode is chosen through `EirTarget(value, input_mode)`, a non-zero `mosquito_delta` is **silently ignored** for `input_mode="eir"` and `input_mode="hbr"`. Note that no warning is raised and no error is thrown, and the EIR comes back unchanged. For the ratio to cancel the bias the method needs a baseline EIR that is independent of the HBR models, and only a prevalence input supplies one. If you already have an EIR or an HBR and want a density change applied to it, scale the HBR yourself and convert. ::: ## See also The full inference surface, every loader, estimator and dataclass the package exposes, is set out in [estiMINT API](api.qmd). Please see [Running scenarios](../06-scenarios/run-scenarios.qmd) for `mosquito_delta` carried through a whole scenario, from the density change to the case counts.
